question: Should kids under 16 be kept off social media?
headline: Experts agree nearly all teens use social media and that heavy use goes with worse mental health. The argument is over whether it causes the harm, and what the fix should be.

settled.text: Nearly all teenagers use social media: up to 95% of US 13- to 17-year-olds say they use at least one platform.

sources.title: Social Media and Youth Mental Health
sources.outlet: U.S. Department of Health and Human Services (Office of the Surgeon General)
sources.quote: Up to 95% of young people aged 13-17 report using a social media platform.

settled.text: Heavy use goes with worse mental health: teens on it more than three hours a day face about double the risk of depression and anxiety symptoms. The major reviews say this doesn't yet prove it causes harm for teens in general.

sources.title: Social Media and Youth Mental Health
sources.outlet: U.S. Department of Health and Human Services (Office of the Surgeon General)
sources.quote: face double the risk of mental health problems including experiencing symptoms of depression and anxiety.

sources.title: To Minimize Harms and Maximize Benefits of Social Media to Adolescent Health, New Report Recommends Setting Industrywide Standards, New Protections Against Harassment
sources.outlet: National Academies of Sciences, Engineering, and Medicine
sources.quote: not enough evidence to say that social media causes changes in adolescent health at the population level.

settled.text: Social media also does real good for some young people, such as staying connected with friends and family, finding community and getting information.

sources.title: Social Media and Youth Mental Health: The U.S. Surgeon General's Advisory (Chapter 1)
sources.outlet: U.S. Surgeon General, via NCBI Bookshelf
sources.quote: Social media can provide benefits for some youth.

sources.title: To Minimize Harms and Maximize Benefits of Social Media to Adolescent Health, New Report Recommends Setting Industrywide Standards, New Protections Against Harassment
sources.outlet: National Academies of Sciences, Engineering, and Medicine
sources.quote: The benefits of social media use suggested by research can include connecting children and adolescents with friends and family.

settled.text: Australia's under-16 ban began on 10 December 2025; three months in, the regulator's own survey found most 10- to 15-year-olds still used at least one banned platform (about 82%, down from 86%).

sources.title: Early days, early insights: SMMA Evaluation, Understanding experiences of social media age restrictions
sources.quote: Despite this reduction, many children who held accounts at baseline had retained them at three months.

sources.title: Australia's under-16 social media ban failing, study shows: What it means
sources.author: Sarah Shamim
sources.quote: continuing to use social media despite being banned from doing so

views.name: Ban accounts under 16
views.summary: Social media is harming a generation of children, and a legal minimum age of 16 that platforms are forced to enforce is the clearest way to give kids their childhood back.
views.who: Jonathan Haidt, Zach Rausch and Ravi Iyer (The Anxious Generation movement); the Australian government under Prime Minister Anthony Albanese and its eSafety Commissioner; parent campaign groups; governments now copying Australia
views.changeMind: Solid follow-up data from Australia showing no improvement in teens' sleep, mood or wellbeing, or a clear rise in harm as kids move to riskier, less-watched apps.

sources.title: What the World Should Learn from Australia's Social Media Law
sources.author: Ravi Iyer, Jonathan Haidt and Zach Rausch
sources.quote: The Australian social media law has not failed.

sources.title: Minimum age for social media access to protect Australian kids
sources.outlet: Minister for Communications / Prime Minister of Australia
sources.author: Anthony Albanese and Michelle Rowland
sources.quote: Social media is doing social harm to our kids.

views.name: Make platforms safer instead
views.summary: The harm comes from how the apps are built, so the law should force tech companies to redesign them to be safe for children rather than simply shutting kids out and letting the companies off the hook.
views.who: Molly Rose Foundation (UK online-safety charity), UNICEF, Amnesty International, Australia's Human Rights and Children's Commissioners
views.changeMind: Evidence that design-safety laws, such as the UK Online Safety Act, fail to reduce harm to children while age limits clearly do.

sources.title: Social media bans are the wrong approach for children
sources.quote: Blunt and simplistic solutions will fail to offer parents and children the safety and wellbeing they are rightly demanding.

sources.title: Age restrictions alone won't keep children safe online
sources.quote: Regulation should not be a substitute for platforms investing in child safety.

views.name: Support kids, don't ban
views.summary: Phones are being blamed for a youth mental-health crisis with deeper causes, so the money and effort should go to counsellors, teachers, families and digital skills rather than bans that can push kids into worse corners online.
views.who: Developmental psychologist Candice Odgers (UC Irvine and Duke); education researchers such as Catherine Smith (University of Melbourne); some youth mental-health advocates
views.changeMind: Well-run studies showing that removing social media actually improves teenagers' mental health.

sources.title: Are we using screens as a scapegoat for teen mental health? (TED Radio Hour transcript)
sources.author: Manoush Zomorodi (host), with Candice Odgers
sources.quote: We need to hire teachers. We need to hire counselors. And we need to pay them well.

sources.title: Australia's under-16 social media ban won't change the reality of growing up online
sources.author: Catherine Smith
sources.quote: blanket bans on technology rarely solve the issues they claim to address.

views.name: Protect privacy and speech
views.summary: Enforcing an age limit means making everyone prove their age with ID or face scans, which endangers privacy and cuts young people off from speech and information, so mandatory age checks do more harm than good.
views.who: Electronic Frontier Foundation (EFF), American Civil Liberties Union (ACLU), digital-rights groups
views.changeMind: Age-check technology that is accurate, stores no personal data, and cannot be used to track or censor people.

sources.title: When No ID Means No Internet: Age Verification and the Right to Access Information
sources.author: Jillian C. York and Sheila B. Lalwani
sources.quote: Age verification technology itself is often inaccurate and privacy-invasive.

sources.title: Lawmakers Renew Push to Regulate Kids' Speech Online Despite Speech Protections
sources.author: Hibah Ansari
sources.quote: broad attempts to regulate speech fail to protect children and violate the First Amendment in the process.

cruxes.question: Does social media cause teens' anxiety and depression?
cruxes.why: If it is a main cause, keeping kids off could help a lot; if it mostly just goes along with other problems, a ban may change little.

cruxes.question: Can age checks work without hurting privacy?
cruxes.why: An under-16 limit only works if apps can tell who is under 16, and that may mean everyone showing ID or their face.

cruxes.question: Do bans push kids to riskier corners online?
cruxes.why: Kids who dodge a ban may end up on less-watched apps, or hide problems from the adults who could help.

cruxes.question: Is it fair to cut off kids who rely on online friends?
cruxes.why: Isolated, disabled or LGBTQ+ teens often find support online, so a ban costs some kids more than others.

wording.assumes: The question treats keeping kids off (access) as the main choice, which takes for granted that the problem is kids being on social media rather than how the apps are designed or what else is going on in kids' lives.
